books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

stimulus.source_note: Treaty of December 30, 1853 (Gadsden Purchase), Article I, as ratified; Article III as ratified set the payment at $10 million. Public domain.
stimulus.text:
Article I. The Mexican Republic agrees to designate the following as her true limits with the United States for the future: . . . Beginning in the Gulf of Mexico, three leagues from land, opposite the mouth of the Rio Grande, as provided in the 5th article of the treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo; thence, as defined in the said article, up the middle of that river to the point where the parallel of 31° 47′ north latitude crosses the same; thence due west one hundred miles; thence south to the parallel of 31° 20′ north latitude; thence along the said parallel of 31° 20′ to the 111th meridian of longitude west of Greenwich; thence in a straight line to a point on the Colorado River twenty English miles below the junction of the Gila and Colorado rivers . . .

[Article III, as ratified, set the payment to Mexico at $10 million.]

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: The Gadsden Purchase is best understood as a sequel to the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo because it did which of the following?

options.text: Returned the Mexican Cession to Mexico in exchange for $10 million in gold.
options.misconception: The purchase added land to the United States; it returned nothing to Mexico.

options.text: Settled a boundary the 1848 treaty had left disputed because its map was faulty.
Ended the Mexican War, which was still being fought in 1853.
options.misconception: The war had ended in 1848; the purchase was a peacetime deal five years later.

options.text: Gave the United States its first land on the Pacific coast.
options.misconception: The United States already held California and Oregon on the Pacific after 1848 and 1846.

rationales.A: The United States paid Mexico and kept the land; nothing was returned.
rationales.B: The 1848 treaty leaned on the faulty Disturnell map, so the two countries read the border differently; the 1853 treaty drew a new line and paid $10 million for the strip.
rationales.C: The war ended with the 1848 treaty; the purchase was a separate peacetime bargain.
rationales.D: California and Oregon already gave the United States a Pacific coast before 1853.
rationales.general:
1. Go back to 1848. The treaty drew the border from the Disturnell map, which misplaced towns and rivers.
2. See the result. Each side read the line differently, and the Mesilla Valley stayed disputed.
3. Watch the fix. In 1853 the United States bought the disputed strip outright and drew a fresh line.
Remember: an old treaty's loose end is a new treaty's business — the Gadsden Purchase finished what Guadalupe Hidalgo left blurry.
